claim: Molecular tension sensors have contributed to a growing understanding of mechanobiology.
source: Molecular tension sensors have contributed to a growing understanding of mechanobiology.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the existence and use of these sensors as described throughout the manuscript.

claim: The limited dynamic range and inability to specify the mechanical sensitivity of molecular tension sensors has hindered their widespread use in diverse contexts.
source: However, the limited dynamic range and inability to specify the mechanical sensitivity of these sensors has hindered their widespread use in diverse contexts.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by the motivation for the study and discussion of limitations in the introduction.

claim: A first principles model describing the mechanical behavior of tension sensors was developed.
source: Guided by the development of a first principles model describing the mechanical behavior of these sensors, we create a collection of sensors that exhibit predictable sensitivities and significantly improved performance in cellulo.
evidence: The development of the model is described in the Results section and Appendix 1.

claim: A collection of sensors with predictable sensitivities and significantly improved performance in cellulo was created.
source: Guided by the development of a first principles model describing the mechanical behavior of these sensors, we create a collection of sensors that exhibit predictable sensitivities and significantly improved performance in cellulo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the creation and testing of multiple vinculin tension sensors with different extensible domains.

claim: A trio of biosensors with distinct force- and extension-sensitivities reveal that an extension-based control paradigm regulates vinculin loading in a variety of mechanical contexts.
source: Utilized in the context of vinculin mechanobiology, a trio of these new biosensors with distinct force- and extension-sensitivities reveal that an extension-based control paradigm regulates vinculin loading in a variety of mechanical contexts.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 and supplementary figures showing conserved extensions but distinct forces across different sensors.

claim: The mechanical behavior of 1020 distinct tension sensor designs was predicted in terms of force and extension.
source: To enable the rational design of molecular tension sensors appropriate for diverse applications, we predict the mechanical behavior, in terms of force and extension, of additional 1020 distinct designs.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1 showing parameter space predictions.

claim: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in migration.
source: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in many fundamentally important biological processes, including migration (Doyle et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2000; Pelham and Wang, 1997), proliferation (Chen et al., 1997; Provenzano and Keely, 2011), differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; Heo et al., 2016; McBeath et al., 2004), and morphogenesis (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Wozniak and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in proliferation.
source: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in many fundamentally important biological processes, including migration (Doyle et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2000; Pelham and Wang, 1997), proliferation (Chen et al., 1997; Provenzano and Keely, 2011), differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; Heo et al., 2016; McBeath et al., 2004), and morphogenesis (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Wozniak and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in differentiation.
source: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in many fundamentally important biological processes, including migration (Doyle et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2000; Pelham and Wang, 1997), proliferation (Chen et al., 1997; Provenzano and Keely, 2011), differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; Heo et al., 2016; McBeath et al., 2004), and morphogenesis (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Wozniak and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in morphogenesis.
source: The ability of cells to generate and respond to mechanical loads is increasingly recognized as a critical driver in many fundamentally important biological processes, including migration (Doyle et al., 2009; Lo et al., 2000; Pelham and Wang, 1997), proliferation (Chen et al., 1997; Provenzano and Keely, 2011), differentiation (Engler et al., 2006; Heo et al., 2016; McBeath et al., 2004), and morphogenesis (Heisenberg and Bellaïche, 2013; Wozniak and Chen, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Most mechanosensitive signaling pathways are thought to have a common basis: the mechanical deformation of load-bearing proteins.
source: While the mechanosensitive signaling pathways enabling these responses are poorly understood, most are thought to have a common basis: the mechanical deformation of load-bearing proteins (Cost et al., 2015; Hoffman et al., 2011; Ju et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Molecular tension sensors leverage the distance-dependence of Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) to measure the extension of and forces across a specific protein of interest.
source: These biosensors, collectively referred to as molecular tension sensors, leverage the distance-dependence of Förster Resonance Energy Transfer (FRET) to measure the extension of and, if properly calibrated, the forces across a specific protein of interest (Austen et al., 2013; Freikamp et al., 2017; Hoffman, 2014; LaCroix et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is a description of how molecular tension sensors work, supported by citations.

claim: The tension across vinculin was shown to regulate a mechanosensitive switch governing the assembly/disassembly dynamics of focal adhesions.
source: For example, using this approach, the tension across vinculin was shown to regulate a mechanosensitive switch governing the assembly/disassembly dynamics of focal adhesions (FAs) (Grashoff et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: A key limitation of FRET-based molecular tension sensors has been the inability to create tension sensors with diverse mechanical sensitivities suitable for a wide variety of biological applications.
source: A key limitation has been the inability to create tension sensors with diverse mechanical sensitivities suitable for a wide variety of biological applications (Freikamp et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and serves as motivation for the current study.

claim: Genetically-encoded molecular tension sensor modules (TSMods) have been created without a priori knowledge of their mechanical sensitivity.
source: To date, genetically-encoded molecular tension sensor modules (TSMods), which are incorporated into various proteins to form distinct tension sensors (Figure 1A), have been created without a priori knowledge of their mechanical sensitivity.
evidence: This describes the current state of the field and is supported by the subsequent discussion of design approaches.

claim: TSMod development has largely relied on a biologically-inspired 'guess-and-check' design approach using naturally-occurring extensible polypeptides or protein domains as deformable elements.
source: TSMod development has largely relied on a biologically-inspired 'guess-and-check' design approach using naturally-occurring extensible polypeptides or protein domains as deformable elements in the FRET-based tension sensors.
evidence: This describes the historical approach to TSMod design.

claim: Calibration measurements of TSMod mechanical sensitivity are typically performed in vitro using highly precise single molecule techniques.
source: Furthermore, despite the use of these sensors to study intracellular processes, calibration measurements of their mechanical sensitivity are typically performed in vitro using highly precise single molecule techniques.
evidence: This describes the typical calibration approach for TSMods.

claim: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN.
source: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), 2–11 pN (Brenner et al., 2016), 3–5 pN (Ringer et al., 2017), 6–8 pN (Austen et al., 2015), or 9–11 pN (Austen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published calibration studies.

claim: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 2–11 pN.
source: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), 2–11 pN (Brenner et al., 2016), 3–5 pN (Ringer et al., 2017), 6–8 pN (Austen et al., 2015), or 9–11 pN (Austen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published calibration studies.

claim: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 3–5 pN.
source: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), 2–11 pN (Brenner et al., 2016), 3–5 pN (Ringer et al., 2017), 6–8 pN (Austen et al., 2015), or 9–11 pN (Austen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published calibration studies.

claim: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 6–8 pN.
source: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), 2–11 pN (Brenner et al., 2016), 3–5 pN (Ringer et al., 2017), 6–8 pN (Austen et al., 2015), or 9–11 pN (Austen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published calibration studies.

claim: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 9–11 pN.
source: Reported force sensitivities of several in vitro calibrated TSMods are 1–6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), 2–11 pN (Brenner et al., 2016), 3–5 pN (Ringer et al., 2017), 6–8 pN (Austen et al., 2015), or 9–11 pN (Austen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published calibration studies.

claim: It is unclear if the reported force ranges of in vitro calibrated TSMods are sufficient for diverse mechanobiological studies.
source: However, it is unclear if these ranges are sufficient for diverse mechanobiological studies, and the applicability of these in vitro calibrations to sensors that are utilized in cellulo has not been verified.
evidence: This expresses uncertainty about the adequacy of current TSMod force ranges.

claim: The applicability of in vitro calibrations to sensors that are utilized in cellulo has not been verified.
source: However, it is unclear if these ranges are sufficient for diverse mechanobiological studies, and the applicability of these in vitro calibrations to sensors that are utilized in cellulo has not been verified.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: TSMod function depends on the Förster radius of the chosen FRET pair.
source: TSMod function depends on the Förster radius of the chosen FRET pair (B) as well as the length (C) and stiffness (D) of the extensible polypeptide domain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: TSMod function depends on the length of the extensible polypeptide domain.
source: TSMod function depends on the Förster radius of the chosen FRET pair (B) as well as the length (C) and stiffness (D) of the extensible polypeptide domain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: TSMod function depends on the stiffness of the extensible polypeptide domain.
source: TSMod function depends on the Förster radius of the chosen FRET pair (B) as well as the length (C) and stiffness (D) of the extensible polypeptide domain.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: Clover-mRuby2 TSMods exhibit 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency than mTFP1-Venus TSMods in fixed cells.
source: This simple substitution yielded a 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency that was observed in fixed (Figure 1E, F) and live cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as well as cell lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Clover-mRuby2 TSMods exhibit 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency than mTFP1-Venus TSMods in live cells.
source: This simple substitution yielded a 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency that was observed in fixed (Figure 1E, F) and live cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as well as cell lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Clover-mRuby2 TSMods exhibit 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency than mTFP1-Venus TSMods in cell lysates.
source: This simple substitution yielded a 12% higher baseline (unloaded) FRET efficiency that was observed in fixed (Figure 1E, F) and live cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), as well as cell lysates (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Minimal versions of Clover (residues 1 – 227) and mRuby2 (residues 3 – 236) exhibit absorbance and emission spectra indistinguishable from their full-length counterparts.
source: Previous work, and our data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), have shown that 'minimal' Clover (residues 1 – 227) and mRuby2 (residues 3 – 236) exhibit absorbance and emission spectra indistinguishable from their full-length counterparts (Austen et al., 2015; Li et al., 1997; Ohashi et al., 2007; Ouyang et al., 2008; Shimozono et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3 and citations to previous work.

claim: TSMods with (GGSGGS)n extensible domains exhibit higher FRET efficiencies than those with (GPGGA)n extensible domains of the same length in cell lysates.
source: Analysis of TSMods in cell lysates showed that those with (GGSGGS)n extensible domains exhibit higher FRET efficiencies than those with (GPGGA)n extensible domains of the same length (Figure 1G), suggesting that (GPGGA)n-based polypeptides are indeed stiffer, and thus force the FPs apart more readily, than (GGSGGS)n-based polypeptides.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: (GPGGA)n-based polypeptides are stiffer than (GGSGGS)n-based polypeptides in vitro.
source: Analysis of TSMods in cell lysates showed that those with (GGSGGS)n extensible domains exhibit higher FRET efficiencies than those with (GPGGA)n extensible domains of the same length (Figure 1G), suggesting that (GPGGA)n-based polypeptides are indeed stiffer, and thus force the FPs apart more readily, than (GGSGGS)n-based polypeptides.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET efficiency data in Figure 1G.

claim: When (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n TSMods were evaluated in cellulo, the FRET efficiency versus length relationships were indistinguishable.
source: However, when (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n TSMods were evaluated in cellulo, the FRET efficiency versus length relationships were indistinguishable, suggesting the polypeptides are exhibiting identical mechanical properties (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n polypeptides exhibit identical mechanical properties in cellulo.
source: However, when (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n TSMods were evaluated in cellulo, the FRET efficiency versus length relationships were indistinguishable, suggesting the polypeptides are exhibiting identical mechanical properties (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is inferred from the indistinguishable FRET-length relationships shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Factors dictating sensor functionality in the absence of applied load can be environmentally sensitive.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that factors dictating sensor functionality in the absence of applied load can be environmentally sensitive, and that the behavior of TSMods observed in vitro may not reflect their behavior in cellulo.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences observed between in vitro and in cellulo measurements.

claim: The behavior of TSMods observed in vitro may not reflect their behavior in cellulo.
source: Together, these data demonstrate that factors dictating sensor functionality in the absence of applied load can be environmentally sensitive, and that the behavior of TSMods observed in vitro may not reflect their behavior in cellulo.
evidence: This is inferred from the differences observed between in vitro and in cellulo measurements.

claim: Both (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n polypeptide mechanics are consistent with unstructured polypeptides.
source: While our modeling efforts indicate that both (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n polypeptide mechanics are consistent with unstructured polypeptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), we only generate calibration predictions for TSMods containing (GGSGGS)n extensible domains because they are also less sensitive to environmental changes.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: (GGSGGS)n extensible domains are less sensitive to environmental changes than (GPGGA)n extensible domains.
source: While our modeling efforts indicate that both (GPGGA)n and (GGSGGS)n polypeptide mechanics are consistent with unstructured polypeptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 6), we only generate calibration predictions for TSMods containing (GGSGGS)n extensible domains because they are also less sensitive to environmental changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that L_P values for (GGSGGS)n are more consistent across environments.

claim: The original vinculin tension sensor (VinTS) reported average loads of ~2.5 pN across vinculin that varied from 1 to 6 pN.
source: Given the original vinculin tension sensor (VinTS) reported average loads of ~2.5 pN across vinculin that varied from 1 to 6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), we choose to further investigate the performance of the TSMod containing the nine-repeat extensible domain, as it exhibits the highest sensitivity in this force regime and is capable of capturing the distribution of the loads on vinculin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is based on previously published data cited from Grashoff et al., 2010.

claim: The TSMod containing the nine-repeat extensible domain exhibits the highest sensitivity in the 1-6 pN force regime.
source: Given the original vinculin tension sensor (VinTS) reported average loads of ~2.5 pN across vinculin that varied from 1 to 6 pN (Grashoff et al., 2010), we choose to further investigate the performance of the TSMod containing the nine-repeat extensible domain, as it exhibits the highest sensitivity in this force regime and is capable of capturing the distribution of the loads on vinculin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by sensitivity analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Vin-/- MEFs expressing either VinTS or opt-VinTS showed indistinguishable cell and FA morphologies.
source: Vin-/- MEFs expressing either VinTS or opt-VinTS showed indistinguishable cell and FA morphologies (Figure 3A,A', C,C', Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: VinTS and opt-VinTS exhibit similar localization within focal adhesions.
source: Furthermore, line scans of acceptor intensity across single FAs indicated similar localization of each sensor (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A'', A''', C'', C''').
evidence: This is supported by line scan data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: VinTS and opt-VinTS exhibit identical biological functionality.
source: These findings indicate that the two sensors exhibit identical biologically functionality.
evidence: This is inferred from the indistinguishable morphologies and localization patterns.

claim: Both VinTS and opt-VinTS report highest loads (lowest FRET efficiency) in the cell periphery.
source: At a subcellular length scale, consistent with our previous findings (Rothenberg et al., 2015), both VinTS and opt-VinTS report highest loads (lowest FRET efficiency) in the cell periphery, and no appreciable tensile loading of vinculin in the cell center (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by FRET images shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Both VinTS and opt-VinTS report no appreciable tensile loading of vinculin in the cell center.
source: At a subcellular length scale, consistent with our previous findings (Rothenberg et al., 2015), both VinTS and opt-VinTS report highest loads (lowest FRET efficiency) in the cell periphery, and no appreciable tensile loading of vinculin in the cell center (Figure 3B,D).
evidence: This is supported by FRET images shown in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: Striking gradients of vinculin tension across single FAs were clearly visible in peripheral FAs of cells expressing opt-VinTS.
source: However, striking gradients of vinculin tension across single FAs were clearly visible in peripheral FAs of cells expressing opt-VinTS (Figure 3D', D'', D''').
evidence: This is supported by images and line scans shown in Figure 3D', D'', D'''.

claim: opt-VinTS exhibits an almost 3-fold improvement in performance compared to the original VinTS (slope = 15.0%/FA vs 5.5%/FA).
source: This analysis revealed an almost 3-fold improvement in the performance opt-VinTS (slope = 15.0%/FA) when compare the original design (slope = 5.5%/FA).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of FRET efficiency changes across FAs.

claim: opt-VinTS is significantly more sensitive than the original VinTS.
source: In total, these results show that, as predicted by the model, opt-VinTS is significantly more sensitive than the original VinTS.
evidence: This is supported by the 3-fold improvement in performance and is consistent with model predictions.

claim: Similar distributions of extension were observed in FAs formed in cells expressing the three different vinculin tension sensors.
source: Intriguingly, we observed similar distributions of extension (Figure 4P), and distinct distributions of tensile forces (Figure 4L) in FAs formed in cells expressing the various sensors.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4P.

claim: Distinct distributions of tensile forces were observed in FAs formed in cells expressing the three different vinculin tension sensors.
source: Intriguingly, we observed similar distributions of extension (Figure 4P), and distinct distributions of tensile forces (Figure 4L) in FAs formed in cells expressing the various sensors.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4L.

claim: Highly loaded FAs in the cell periphery exhibit conserved gradients in extension rather than force.
source: Furthermore, highly loaded FAs in the cell periphery exhibit conserved gradients in extension rather than force (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by line scan data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vinculin extension-control is robust to short-term inhibition of ROCK-mediated cytoskeletal contractility.
source: First, treatment of cells with the Y-27632 showed that vinculin extension-control is robust to short-term inhibition of ROCK-mediated cytoskeletal contractility (Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: Vinculin extension-control does not require vinculin-talin interactions.
source: Secondly, vinculin extension-control does not require vinculin-talin interactions, as assessed through the introduction of a point mutation (A50I) in the three versions of VinTS (Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 5 and 6.

claim: Extension-based control still occurs on substrates of physiologically-relevant 10 kPa stiffness.
source: Finally, we observed that extension-based control still occurs on substrates of physiologically-relevant 10 kPa stiffness (Figure 4—figure supplements 7 and 8).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 7 and 8.

claim: Loads across vinculin are exclusively governed by an extension-based control rather than a force-based control paradigm.
source: Together, these results strongly suggest that loads across vinculin are exclusively governed by an extension-based control rather than the more commonly assumed force-based control paradigm.
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent observation of conserved extensions and distinct forces across multiple experimental conditions.

claim: A force input to the entire FA structure always resulted in force-based control within the sensor elements.
source: Regardless of the relative abundance of the elements or their respective stiffness, a force input to the entire structure always resulted in force-based control within the sensor elements.
evidence: This is based on simulations using the FA structural model described in Appendix 2.

claim: An extension input to the entire FA structure gave rise to both extension-controlled and force-controlled regimes in the sensor elements.
source: In contrast, an extension input to the entire structure, as might arise due to defined myosin motor step size (Murphy et al., 2001) or actin polymerization (Peskin et al., 1993), gave rise to both extension-controlled and force-controlled regimes in the sensor elements.
evidence: This is based on simulations using the FA structural model and is supported by citations.

claim: Extension-controlled loading of the sensor element is more strongly observed when the sensor element is relatively soft and/or in low abundance.
source: The extension-controlled loading of the sensor element is more strongly observed when the sensor element is relatively soft and/or in low abundance, otherwise a force-controlled system is predicted (Figure 4—figure supplement 9D).
evidence: This is based on simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9D.

claim: In the extension-controlled regime, the FA structural model predicts a linear relationship between sensor element stiffness and the force borne by the three sensor elements.
source: Furthermore, in the extension-controlled regime, this simple model also predicts the linear relationship between sensor element stiffness and the force borne by the three sensor elements that was observed in all control paradigm experiments (Figure 4—figure supplement 9E).
evidence: This is based on simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 9E.

claim: Protein extension, instead of applied force, might be a key mechanical variable in some mechanosensitive processes.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that protein extension, instead of applied force, might be a key mechanical variable in some mechanosensitive processes.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observations and modeling results.

claim: The rational design and implementation of future tension sensors with diverse and a priori specified properties is now possible.
source: With these roadmaps as a guide, the rational design and implementation of future tension sensors with diverse and a priori specified properties is now possible.
evidence: This is inferred from the availability of the roadmaps and calibration model.

claim: Context-dependent mechanical behaviors were observed in TSMods, as responses for the same constructs were mechanically distinct in in vitro and in cellulo experiments.
source: Surprisingly, we observed context-dependent mechanical behaviors in TSMods, as responses for the same constructs were mechanically distinct in in vitro and in cellulo experiments.
evidence: This is based on the differences in L_P values measured in different environments.

claim: Crowding effects are less likely to explain the variety of reported mechanics in TSMods.
source: However, we surmise that crowding effects are less likely for two reasons. First, previous work has shown that crowding effects are more prominent at longer linker lengths (Ohashi et al., 2007). Additionally, in our in vitro and in cellulo systems, we observed that (GPGGA)n-based polypeptides exhibit higher FRET in vitro, while (GGSGGS)n polypeptides exhibited lower FRET in these conditions.
evidence: This is inferred from the observed patterns of FRET differences and is supported by a citation.

claim: The optimized vinculin sensor exhibited a marked increase in the ability to detect asymmetric distributions of molecular tension within single FAs.
source: This optimized sensor exhibited a marked increase in the ability to detect asymmetric distributions of molecular tension within single FAs.
evidence: This is supported by the improved performance shown in Figure 3.

claim: Similar tension asymmetries have been observed external to the cell using high resolution traction force microscopy.
source: Similar tension asymmetries have been observed external to the cell using both high resolution traction force microscopy (Legant et al., 2013; Plotnikov et al., 2012) and extracellular tension sensors (Blakely et al., 2014; Morimatsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Similar tension asymmetries have been observed external to the cell using extracellular tension sensors.
source: Similar tension asymmetries have been observed external to the cell using both high resolution traction force microscopy (Legant et al., 2013; Plotnikov et al., 2012) and extracellular tension sensors (Blakely et al., 2014; Morimatsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Gradients in vinculin tension have been reported in cells adhered to micropost arrays.
source: Intracellularly, gradients in vinculin tension have been reported in cells adhered to micropost arrays, although tension asymmetries were mainly attributed to the presence of discontinuous substrates (Sarangi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published work.

claim: Asymmetric molecular loads are detectable without the need for super-resolution imaging and are transmitted through vinculin even on continuous substrates.
source: We show that these asymmetric molecular loads are detectable without the need for super-resolution imaging and are transmitted through vinculin even on continuous substrates.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3 using conventional microscopy on glass substrates.

claim: Once vinculin is activated through interactions with talin and/or actin, it is pulled until a given extension is achieved, not a set force.
source: Specifically, once vinculin is activated through interactions with talin and/or actin (Bakolitsa et al., 2004; Bois et al., 2006; Chen et al., 2006a), it is pulled until a given extension is achieved, not a set force.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension-control paradigm observed in the experiments and is supported by citations.

claim: The load-dependent maintenance of vinculin activation may be determined by vinculin extension, rather than force.
source: Thus, the load-dependent maintenance of vinculin activation (Dumbauld et al., 2013) may be determined by vinculin extension, rather than force.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension-control paradigm and is supported by a citation.

claim: Extension may be the most pertinent biophysical variable governing the initiation of vinculin-dependent and possibly other mechanosensitive signaling pathways.
source: More broadly, extension may be the most pertinent biophysical variable governing the initiation of vinculin-dependent and possibly other mechanosensitive signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension-control paradigm observed for vinculin.

claim: The extension-control paradigm is consistent with reports that cells induce similar strains within extracellular environments of differing stiffness.
source: Extrapolated to longer length scales, this extension-control paradigm agrees well with reports that cells induce similar strains within extracellular environments of differing stiffness (Lin et al., 2018; Saez et al., 2005) and that strain determines the activation of touch-sensitive channels in in vivo models (Eastwood et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The extension-control paradigm is consistent with reports that strain determines the activation of touch-sensitive channels in in vivo models.
source: Extrapolated to longer length scales, this extension-control paradigm agrees well with reports that cells induce similar strains within extracellular environments of differing stiffness (Lin et al., 2018; Saez et al., 2005) and that strain determines the activation of touch-sensitive channels in in vivo models (Eastwood et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Measurements of force in an extension-control regime will be dependent on the stiffness of the sensor design.
source: However, we note that measurements of force in an extension-control regime will be dependent on the stiffness of the sensor design.
evidence: This is inferred from the extension-control paradigm and the force-extension relationship.

claim: Sensor stiffness dependence could be one possible reason for a variety of forces reported by different sensor designs for the same protein.
source: We speculate that this could be one possible reason for a variety of forces reported by different sensor designs for the same protein (Erickson, 2017).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation.
